q: how do i predict a crop
a: Go to the Predict Crop page, enter your soil values (N, P, K), temperature, humidity, pH, and rainfall, then click Get Recommendation. The model will suggest the best crop with confidence scores.
This is a Precision Crop Recommendation System that uses a hybrid ML model (LightGBM + XGBoost + CatBoost) to recommend the best crop based on your soil and climate conditions.
The model uses a stacked ensemble of LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost as base learners, with Logistic Regression as the meta-learner. It analyzes 7 input features plus 5 engineered ratio features.
Stacking combines multiple models: LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost generate predictions via 5-fold cross-validation, then a Logistic Regression meta-learner combines them for the final prediction.

q: what features does the model use
a: The model uses 7 raw features (N, P, K, temperature, humidity, pH, rainfall) plus 5 engineered features (N_P_ratio, N_K_ratio, P_K_ratio, NPK_sum, temp_humid) for a total of 12 features.
The hybrid stacked ensemble achieves very high accuracy on the test set, typically above 99%. Check the Model Insights page for exact metrics.
The Model Insights page shows accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, top-3 accuracy, and log loss. It also displays confusion matrices, SHAP plots, and model comparison charts.
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) shows which features most influenced a prediction. Higher SHAP values mean that feature had more impact on the crop recommendation.

22 crops: Apple, Banana, Blackgram, Chickpea, Coconut, Coffee, Cotton, Grapes, Jute, Kidney Beans, Lentil, Maize, Mango, Moth Beans, Mung Bean, Muskmelon, Orange, Papaya, Pigeon Peas, Pomegranate, Rice, Watermelon.
Rice requires high humidity (80-85%), standing water, clayey or loamy soil, pH 5.5-7.0, rainfall 150-300mm, and warm temperatures 20-30°C. It's ideal for tropical and subtropical regions.
Wheat is not in our 22-crop dataset, but generally it grows in cool climates with well-drained loamy soil, pH 6.0-7.5, moderate rainfall, and temperatures between 15-25°C.
Maize requires warm weather (18-27°C), well-drained loamy soil, pH 5.5-7.5, and moderate to high rainfall (60-120mm). It needs good drainage and full sunlight.
Cotton requires long warm summers (21-30°C), deep black soil, pH 5.8-8.0, moderate rainfall (50-100mm), and full sunshine. It's suited to semi-arid tropical regions.
Coffee needs a subtropical climate (18-24°C), high humidity, moderate rainfall (150-250mm), well-drained acidic loam soil with pH 5.0-6.5, and partial shade.
Mango needs a tropical climate (24-30°C), deep loamy well-drained soil, pH 5.5-7.5, rainfall 75-250mm, and seasonal dry spells for proper flowering.
Banana thrives in tropical climates with high humidity, consistent rainfall throughout the year, rich loamy soil, and temperatures between 25-30°C.
Apple grows best in cool climates with well-drained loamy soil, requires cold winters for dormancy, pH 5.5-6.5, and temperatures between 10-25°C.
Grapes thrive in Mediterranean climates with hot dry summers, well-drained sandy soil, pH 6.0-7.0, moderate rainfall, and temperatures between 15-35°C.
Coconut palms require tropical climate, sandy well-drained soil, coastal humid winds, pH 5.5-8.0, rainfall 100-250mm, and temperatures between 25-30°C.
Orange grows in subtropical climates with warm sunny conditions, well-drained fertile soil, pH 6.0-7.5, moderate rainfall, and temperatures between 15-30°C.
Watermelon needs hot sunny weather, a long frost-free season, sandy well-drained soil, pH 6.0-7.0, and temperatures between 25-35°C.
Papaya is a fast-growing tropical fruit requiring rich moist loamy soil, full sun, pH 6.0-7.0, good drainage, and temperatures between 25-30°C.
Chickpea grows in dry cool conditions, is highly drought-tolerant, ideal for Rabi season, with pH 6.0-9.0 and temperatures between 15-25°C.
Lentil is a cool-season pulse crop highly tolerant to drought, suited to semi-arid regions, with well-drained loamy soil and pH 6.0-8.0.
Jute grows best in warm humid climates with loamy alluvial soil, high monsoonal rainfall (150-250mm), and temperatures between 25-35°C.
Pomegranate thrives in semi-arid to arid regions, tolerates alkaline well-drained soils, pH 5.5-7.5, and temperatures between 25-35°C.
Nitrogen (N) is a key macronutrient for plant growth. It promotes leaf and stem development. Typical values in the dataset range from 0-140 kg/ha depending on the crop.
Phosphorus (P) supports root development, flowering, and fruiting. It helps plants convert nutrients into usable building blocks. Values typically range 5-145 kg/ha.
Potassium (K) helps plants resist diseases, aids water regulation, and improves crop quality. Values in the dataset range from 5-205 kg/ha.
NPK stands for Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium — the three primary macronutrients essential for plant growth. Each crop has different NPK requirements.
Soil pH measures acidity/alkalinity on a 0-14 scale. Most crops prefer pH 5.5-7.5. Acidic soils (pH<6) suit coffee and tea; alkaline soils (pH>7) suit chickpea and cotton.
Humidity is the moisture content in the air, measured as a percentage. High humidity (80%+) suits rice and banana; low humidity suits chickpea and lentil.
Rainfall is the amount of precipitation in millimeters. Some crops like rice need 150-300mm, while drought-tolerant crops like chickpea need much less.

q: what temperature is best for crops
a: It varies: cool-season crops (apple, lentil) prefer 10-25°C; warm-season crops (rice, cotton) prefer 20-35°C; tropical crops (banana, papaya) prefer 25-30°C.
Rice, Banana, Coconut, and Jute all thrive in high humidity (80%+). Rice especially needs consistently high humidity throughout its growing season.
Chickpea, Lentil, Moth Beans, and Muskmelon prefer drier conditions with lower humidity levels.
Rice (150-300mm), Jute (150-250mm), Coffee (150-250mm), and Banana need high consistent rainfall for optimal growth.
Chickpea, Lentil, Moth Beans, and Mung Bean are drought-tolerant crops that can thrive with minimal rainfall.

q: which crop grows in acidic soil
a: Coffee (pH 5.0-6.5), Apple (pH 5.5-6.5), and Rice (pH 5.5-7.0) prefer slightly acidic soil conditions.

q: which crop grows in alkaline soil
a: Cotton (pH 5.8-8.0), Chickpea (pH 6.0-9.0), and Pomegranate tolerate alkaline soil conditions well.
Watermelon, Muskmelon, Coconut, and Groundnut do well in sandy, well-drained soils.
Rice and Jute thrive in clayey soil as it retains water well. Cotton also does well in deep black clay soil.
Most crops prefer loamy soil: Maize, Mango, Coffee, Banana, Papaya, and many others grow well in rich loamy soil.
Feature engineering creates new features from existing ones. This model creates N_P_ratio, N_K_ratio, P_K_ratio, NPK_sum, and temp_humid from the 7 raw inputs to improve predictions.
N_P_ratio = N / (P + 1). It measures the Nitrogen-to-Phosphorus balance in soil, which is important for determining crop suitability.
NPK_sum = N + P + K. It represents the total macronutrient load in the soil, giving an overall picture of soil fertility.
temp_humid = temperature × humidity. It's a heat-moisture stress index that captures the combined effect of temperature and humidity on crop growth.
LightGBM is a fast gradient boosting framework. In this model, it's used as a base learner with 500 estimators, 0.05 learning rate, and 63 leaves.
XGBoost is an optimized gradient boosting library. Here it's a base learner with 300 estimators and 0.05 learning rate.
CatBoost is a gradient boosting library that handles categorical features natively. It's used with 300 iterations and depth 6 in this model.
Logistic Regression is used as the meta-learner in the stacking ensemble. It combines the predictions from LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost to make the final crop prediction.
5-fold cross-validation splits training data into 5 parts, trains on 4 and validates on 1, rotating through all folds. This ensures robust evaluation and prevents overfitting during stacking.
A confusion matrix shows how well the model classifies each crop. The diagonal shows correct predictions; off-diagonal shows misclassifications. Check Model Insights for the chart.
Precision measures how many predicted positive cases were actually correct. High precision means fewer false positives.
Recall measures how many actual positive cases were correctly identified. High recall means fewer false negatives.
F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It balances both metrics and is useful when you need a single measure of model performance.
Log loss measures how well the model's predicted probabilities match actual outcomes. Lower log loss means more confident and accurate probability predictions.
Top-3 accuracy checks if the correct crop is among the model's top 3 predictions. This is useful because the second or third choice may still be a viable crop.
The system supports 22 crop types, with 100 training samples each (2,200 total samples in the dataset).
7 raw input features (N, P, K, temperature, humidity, pH, rainfall) plus 5 engineered features, totaling 12 features used by the model.
The dataset contains 2,200 samples (100 samples for each of the 22 crop classes), split 80/20 for training and testing.
The dataset is Crop_recommendation.csv with 2,200 rows and 8 columns (7 features + label). Each crop class has 100 balanced samples.
StandardScaler normalizes features to have zero mean and unit variance. It's applied to distance-based models like SVM and KNN to ensure all features contribute equally.
The hybrid stacked ensemble (LightGBM + XGBoost + CatBoost → Logistic Regression) typically achieves the highest accuracy, outperforming individual baseline models.

The Schemes page lists Indian government agricultural schemes. You can filter by state, category, farmer type, income level, and land size.
Government schemes are programs like PM-KISAN (income support) and PMFBY (crop insurance) that provide financial assistance to farmers.
PM-KISAN provides income support of Rs 6,000 per year to eligible farmer families through direct benefit transfer in three installments.
PMFBY (Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana) is a crop insurance scheme that provides coverage for yield loss due to natural calamities.
Summer crops include Watermelon, Muskmelon, Cotton, Maize, and Mung Bean. These crops thrive in hot weather with adequate irrigation.
Winter (Rabi) crops include Chickpea, Lentil, and Wheat. These crops prefer cool temperatures and are harvested in spring.
Monsoon (Kharif) crops include Rice, Maize, Jute, Cotton, and Pigeon Peas. They benefit from heavy monsoon rainfall.
Kharif season (June-October) coincides with the monsoon. Crops like Rice, Maize, Cotton, and Jute are planted during this season.
Rabi season (October-March) is the winter cropping season. Crops like Chickpea, Lentil, and Wheat are grown during this period.
Improve soil by adding organic compost, rotating crops (especially legumes for nitrogen fixation), maintaining proper pH with lime or sulfur, and ensuring good drainage.
Crop rotation means growing different crops in sequence on the same land. It improves soil health, reduces pests, and maintains nutrient balance. Legumes are great for fixing nitrogen.
Organic farming avoids synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, using natural methods like compost, crop rotation, and biological pest control for sustainable agriculture.
Get a soil test from your local agricultural extension office. They measure N, P, K levels, pH, organic matter, and micronutrients. Enter these values in our Predict Crop page.
Drip irrigation delivers water directly to plant roots through tubes, reducing water waste by 30-50% compared to flood irrigation. Ideal for water-scarce regions.
Nitrogen fixation is done by legumes (blackgram, mung bean, lentil, chickpea, pigeon peas) which host bacteria that convert atmospheric nitrogen into soil nutrients.
Blackgram is a legume suited to warm semi-arid conditions. It fixes nitrogen in soil, improving fertility. It prefers temperatures of 25-35°C and moderate rainfall.
Mung bean is a short-season legume suited to warm humid regions. It improves soil fertility through nitrogen fixation and matures in 60-90 days.
Kidney beans prefer well-drained fertile soil with moderate temperatures between 15-25°C, pH 6.0-7.5, and adequate but not excessive rainfall.
Moth beans are highly drought-resistant and perfectly suited to the hot arid zones of India. They require minimal water and tolerate poor soils.
Pigeon peas (Arhar/Tur) are drought-tolerant, nitrogen-fixing legumes suited to semi-arid tropical regions. They're a major pulse crop in India.
Muskmelon needs warm temperatures (25-35°C), dry weather during fruiting, and light sandy well-drained soil. It's a summer crop that needs full sunlight.

q: what is the best soil type
a: Loamy soil is generally the best as it retains moisture while providing good drainage. However, specific crops prefer clay (rice), sandy (watermelon), or black soil (cotton).
In SHAP plots, each dot is a sample. Red means high feature value, blue means low. Features at the top have the most impact on predictions. Right side means positive impact.
A beeswarm SHAP plot shows each feature's impact direction per sample. Dots spread right indicate the feature pushes toward a prediction; left means it pushes against.
Feature importance ranks which inputs matter most for predictions. In this model, features like humidity, rainfall, and pH typically rank highest.
